lesson.title: Network Interfaces: Where a Host Meets Its Link
lesson.summary: Defines the network interface as the hardware and software point where a host attaches to a communication link, and explains why a single host can have multiple interfaces.
lesson.body:
A host does not connect to a communication link directly through thin air, it connects through a specific piece of hardware, and often accompanying software, dedicated to that job. This attachment point is called a network interface. A network interface is what physically or wirelessly transmits and receives data on behalf of a host over a particular communication link. A wired Ethernet port and its associated circuitry form a network interface. A WiFi radio and antenna form a different kind of network interface. Every time a host sends data out onto a link or receives data coming in from one, it does so through one of its network interfaces.

It is easy to assume a host has just one interface, but many hosts have several at once. A modern laptop typically has both a WiFi interface and a wired Ethernet interface, even if only one is actively in use at a given moment. A smartphone commonly has a cellular interface and a WiFi interface. A server in a data center might have multiple wired interfaces for redundancy or to handle very high traffic volumes. Each interface is a separate attachment point to a separate link, or at least a separate connection, and each is tracked and addressed independently by the host's operating system, which is why the next two sections introduce two different kinds of addresses, the MAC address and the IP address, both of which are properties assigned to a specific interface rather than to the host as a whole.

This interface by interface view resolves a question that might otherwise be confusing: if a host can have multiple addresses, which one is the host's address? The honest answer is that a host does not truly have a single address at all, each of its interfaces does. A laptop connected to both WiFi and Ethernet simultaneously would have two different addresses active at the same time, one per interface, and data destined for the laptop would need to arrive at whichever interface's address it was sent to.

Consider a worked example. Your laptop is sitting on your desk, connected to your home network over WiFi. Its WiFi network interface, referred to in many operating systems by a name like wlan0 or Wi-Fi, is the piece of hardware handling every bit sent and received. If you then plug in an Ethernet cable, your laptop's separate wired interface, often called eth0 or Ethernet, activates and can carry traffic too, entirely independently of the WiFi interface. Depending on how your operating system is configured, the laptop might now use the wired interface preferentially, since wired connections are typically faster and more stable, while the WiFi interface sits idle but ready.

Because so much of addressing and forwarding in a network is really about identifying interfaces rather than hosts in the abstract, understanding the network interface as its own concept, distinct from the host it belongs to, sets up the next two sections cleanly: MAC addresses and IP addresses are both, precisely speaking, addresses of interfaces.
